query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Employ contactless electromagnetic levitation (EML) combined with fast scanning calorimetry (FSC) to measure melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamics in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) without crucible-induced artifacts.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy specimens (e.g., fcc Cantor alloy, bcc alloys) prepared by standard methods, as in the paper.
generation.intervention: Replace traditional differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) in a crucible with an EML-FSC setup that suspends the alloy sample in a high-purity inert gas stream.
generation.conditions: High-vacuum or high-purity inert gas (e.g., argon) atmosphere; heating rates comparable to FSC; electromagnetic levitation conditions optimized for metallic samples; temperature range from room temperature to above the solidus.
generation.structural_mediator: Elimination of physical contact with a crucible and the associated chemical reactions that can alter cp curves near melting.
generation.mechanism: Without contact, the sample avoids reactions with container materials (e.g., Pt-Rh crucibles or ceramic inlays) that were observed to truncate or distort heat capacity curves in the paper. In an EML environment, the thermal events such as latent heat absorption and volume expansion occur in a chemically inert environment. The fast scanning capability minimizes superheating and provides rapid thermal equilibration, allowing accurate resolution of the melting temperature and associated thermodynamic parameters.
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate and reproducible determination of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change; expected reduction of measurement error by at least 5–10% relative to conventional DSC methods affected by crucible interactions.
generation.baseline: Conventional DSC measurements as reported in the paper, which show discrepancies (e.g., a 70 K shift in fcc-noble alloy and issues with bcc/hcp alloys due to chemical reactions).
generation.boundary: Applicability may be limited to HEAs with sufficient electromagnetic response for stable levitation; alloys with low electrical conductivity might require alternative methodologies.
generation.uncertainty: While EML-FSC is proven for pure metals and simpler alloys, uncertainty remains in scaling the method across the entire diverse compositional space of HEAs.

cited_evidence.text: Many elements, and therefore a high value of configurational entropy, can lead to a more stable solid-solution phase with randomly distributed atoms []. A solid-solution phase with statistically distributed atoms in the crystal lattice is claimed to lead to interesting and outstanding properties, e.g., high hardness, wear resistance, high temperature strength and stability, sluggish diffusion, oxidation and corrosion resistance [,]. Yeh et al. [] named four core effects, which are characteristic for microstructures and properties of high entropy alloys: the formation of one random solid-solution phase to reach a high entropy effect []; severe lattice distortion in the random solid-solution []; sluggish diffusion kinetics [,]; the so called “cocktail effect” []. Nevertheless the major part of investigated alloys with compositional requirements of high entropy alloys do not form single solid-solutions, but consist of several, mostly intermetallic phases, which can be brittle, difficult to process. This observation particularly disagrees with the crucial issue of a single-phase microstructure.

Single-crystalline (SX) nickel and SX-Cantor alloy (favored equiatomic composition of Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) were cast using a proprietary Bridgman investment casting furnace. Cylindrical specimens (Ø 5 mm, height 1 mm) were then cut out of the rods by electrical discharge machining (EDM). All other alloys were in poly-crystalline state. The bcc-alloys were provided by Senkov et al. [], the noble metal alloy by Freudenberger et al. [] and the hcp-alloy by Feuerbacher et al. []. The recast layer of the EDM samples was removed by etching and the base of all samples was finely ground with SiC paper up to 2000 grit to ensure good thermal contact to the DSC-sensor. All materials tested several times showed good reproducibility in their DSC-signal, even at different heating rates of 10 K/min and 20 K/min respectively. Except for pure nickel all materials belong to the high entropy alloys group. They form a single-phase microstructure and contain at least four elements in desired, near equiatomic composition. The single-phase solid-solution has been confirmed by the authors using X-ray diffraction experiments. Homogenization of the samples was reached by very slow cooling rates after melting

fields.hypothesis: Integrate containerless aerodynamic levitation with simultaneous in situ calorimetry and neutron (or synchrotron) diffraction to directly capture the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase structure of HEAs. By eliminating container interactions, the transient thermal events and structural changes during melting can be measured rapidly and with high accuracy across HEA compositions.
fields.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in as-cast form, prepared as small spherical samples to facilitate levitation.
fields.intervention: Utilize an aerodynamic levitator to heat the sample using a CO2 laser while performing high-speed calorimetric and diffraction measurements concurrently.
fields.conditions: Experiments conducted in inert gas atmosphere at controlled pressures to minimize oxidation; heating rates controlled to allow near equilibrium at transition; applicable to a range of HEA compositions, especially those with Al and transition metals.
fields.structural_mediator: The microstructure of HEAs, which exhibits both short-range and long-range order (as previously revealed by neutron scattering in Al-containing HEAs, e.g., record_id PMC6207727::web::022), provides distinct diffraction peaks that change at melting.
fields.mechanism: Eliminating container-induced heterogeneous nucleation via levitation improves measurement accuracy. Simultaneous calorimetry records the latent heat release, while diffraction detects the disappearance of solid-phase order and the emergence of liquid-phase signatures. This dual-modal approach facilitates precise determination of melting temperature, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion, and volume changes due to the abrupt shift in density as captured by the evolving diffraction pattern.
fields.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of melting properties with deviations of only a few percent compared to known standards; clear detection of the onset of melting and associated latent heat plateau in cooling curves, with diffraction confirming complete loss of crystalline order.
fields.baseline: Traditional container-based DSC or drop-tube experiments that can suffer from contamination and undercooling artifacts.
fields.boundary: May be limited for HEAs with extremely high reactivity or when the sample size is too large for effective levitation.
fields.uncertainty: While the method is expected to reduce systematic errors, the exact precision level across the entire HEA composition space requires experimental validation.

measurements: Volume change (density change) inferred from diffraction peak shifts
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated measurement does not produce a consistent latent heat plateau and diffraction evidence of melting (or if it shows significantly larger deviation from baseline methods without a clear rationale), then the hypothesis that the containerless dual technique accurately captures the thermodynamic transition is refuted.

top3.builds_on: the observation from the paper that crucible reactions impede accurate high-temperature measurements (e.g., truncated cp curves and ambiguous melting intervals).
top3.what_is_new: A combined DSC and dilatometry setup with specially engineered sample encapsulation to directly capture both thermal and volumetric signatures of fusion in HEAs, rather than relying solely on DSC.

fields.hypothesis: Integrate a high-temperature, inert-atmosphere DSC with advanced sample encapsulation (using chemically inert coatings) and simultaneous in-situ dilatometry to accurately determine the melting point, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and associated volume change in HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: Conventionally prepared single-phase HEA specimens (e.g., fcc alloys, bcc alloys) with known crystallographic structures.
fields.intervention: Coat DSC sample crucibles and potentially the sample surfaces with an ultra-thin layer of an inert material (for instance, a B2O3 or high-purity alumina coating) to prevent alloy–crucible reactions. Couple this setup with an in-situ dilatometer to capture volumetric changes during melting.
fields.conditions: High-purity inert gas (e.g., Ar 5.0) flush at controlled high flow rates; temperature scanning rates (10–20 K/min) as in the paper; integration of DSC and dilatometry data acquisition.
fields.structural_mediator: Suppression of chemical interaction at the sample–crucible interface minimizes artifacts in the heat flow signal, while the dilatometry module enables real-time monitoring of volume expansion known to accompany melting.
fields.mechanism: By chemically isolating the sample from reactive crucible surfaces (as observed in the paper for bcc-5 component and hcp alloys) and controlling the atmosphere, the measurement avoids spurious peaks and drift in cp. Simultaneously, in-situ dilatometry captures the sudden volume change at melting, allowing direct determination of liquid-phase properties that are otherwise inferred indirectly.
fields.predicted_outcome: Improved accuracy (potentially within ±2–3% of true values) in determining melting temperature, latent heat, and entropy of fusion along with a quantifiable volume change signature at melting. This method is expected to work across a broad range of HEA compositions.
fields.baseline: Standard DSC measurements with uncoated crucibles which, as reported in the paper, suffer from reaction-induced inaccuracies, especially for bcc and hcp alloys.
fields.boundary: The approach is applicable for alloys where suitable inert coatings are available and stable up to the melting temperature; extremely reactive HEAs or those with high diffusion rates at high temperature might still pose challenges.
fields.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement may vary between different HEA systems and depends on the long-term chemical stability of the protective coatings under high temperatures.
